No polite title, no fuss — just family, plain and direct, the way you describe your own grandmother to someone else.

A child mishears the rhythm as <reading>そぼ</reading>, the word for grandmother, and now everyone at the water's edge calls her the <reading>sew-bow</reading> lady who happens to be somebody's grandmother too.

Nobody in the family questions this anymore. That's just what your uncle does.

It's not a stranger — it's your uncle, and that startled gasp is exactly <reading>おじ</reading>: <reading>oh, gee</reading>, uncle, fancy meeting you up here.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, an aunt turns up every New Year wrapped in an absurd sheep-print scarf. The temple cats scatter, certain a sheep has invaded their mossy steps. Flustered, she throws up both hands and calls out across the courtyard — that startled, scarf-wrapped arrival is exactly who aunt means.
items.reading_mnemonic: As the cats bolt, she cries <reading>Oh, baa!</reading> — sheep noise, not sheep, just her own flustered yelp. That startled cry, <reading>おば</reading>, is the exact sound of an aunt arriving at Grandma Kane's shrine every single year, scarf and all.
